title: De Divinatione
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi053.perseus-lat3, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Magnifica quaedam res et salutaris, si modo est ulla, quaque proxime ad deorum vim natura mortalis possit accedere. Itaque ut alia nos melius multa quam Graeci, sic huic praestantissimae rei nomen nostri a divis, Graeci, ut Plato interpretatur, a furore duxerunt.
passages.english: [It is] a magnificent and salutary thing, if only it exists at all, and one by which mortal nature might come closest to the power of the gods. And so, just as we [Romans have done] many other things better than the Greeks, so our ancestors derived the name of this most excellent thing from the gods (*divi*), while the Greeks, as Plato explains it, derived it from madness.
passages.notes: Plays on divinatio from divi, and Greek mantikē from mania (madness), per Plato's etymology in the Phaedrus.

passages.original: An medicina ars non putanda est? quam tamen multa fallunt. Quid? gubernatores nonne falluntur? An Achivorum exercitus et tot navium rectores non ita profecti sunt ab Ilio, ut profectione laeti piscium lasciviam intuerentur, ut ait Pacuvius, nec tuendi satietas capere posset?Ínterea prope iam óccidente sóle inhorrescít mare,Ténebrae conduplicántur noctisque ét nimbum occaecát nigror. Num igitur tot clarissimorum ducum regumque naufragium sustulit artem gubernandi?
passages.english: Or is medicine not to be thought an art? Yet many things lead it astray. What about this? Are helmsmen not deceived? Did not the army of the Achaeans and the captains of so many ships set out from Ilium in such a way that, glad at their departure, they watched the sporting of the fish, as Pacuvius says, and could not have their fill of looking? "Meanwhile, with the sun now almost setting, the sea grows rough, / the darkness doubles, and the blackness of night and storm-cloud blinds [them]." Did the shipwreck of so many most famous leaders and kings, then, abolish the art of steering?

passages.original: Carent autem arte ii, qui non ratione aut coniectura observatis ac notatis signis, sed concitatione quadam animi aut soluto liberoque motu futura praesentiunt, quod et somniantibus saepe contingit et non numquam vaticinantibus per furorem, ut Bacis Boeotius, ut Epimenides Cres, ut Sibylla Erythraea. Cuius generis oracla etiam habenda sunt, non ea, quae aequatis sortibus ducuntur, sed illa, quae instinctu divino adflatuque funduntur; etsi ipsa sors contemnenda non est, si et auctoritatem habet vetustatis, ut eae sunt sortes, quas e terra editas accepimus;
passages.english: Those, however, are without art who foresee the future not by reasoning or conjecture from signs observed and noted, but by a certain excitement of the mind or by a free and unrestrained movement [of it]. This often happens to people dreaming, and sometimes to those who prophesy through frenzy, like Bacis of Boeotia, like Epimenides of Crete, like the Erythraean Sibyl. To this kind must also be assigned oracles, not those that are drawn by evened lots, but those that are poured forth by divine impulse and inspiration; although the lot itself is not to be despised, if it also has the authority of antiquity, as do those lots which, we are told, sprang forth from the earth;
passages.notes: 'aequatis sortibus': lots made equal (so that the draw is fair); sense somewhat uncertain.

passages.original: Num te ad fabulas revoco vel nostrorum vel Graecorum poëtarum? Narrat enim et apud Ennium Vestalis illa: Eccita cum tremulis anus attulit artubus lumen,Talia tum memorat lacrimans exterrita somno:“Eurydica prognata, pater quam noster amavit,Vires vitaque corpus meum nunc deserit omne.Nam me visus homo pulcher per amoena salicta Et ripas raptare locosque novos;
passages.english: Am I calling you back to the tales of the poets, either ours or the Greeks'? For in Ennius too that Vestal tells her story: "When the old woman, roused, had brought a lamp with trembling limbs, / then, weeping and terrified out of sleep, she recounts these things: / 'Daughter of Eurydice, whom our father loved, / strength and life now abandon my whole body. / For a handsome man seemed to carry me off through pleasant willow groves / and banks and unfamiliar places;
passages.notes: The Vestal is Ilia, mother of Romulus and Remus; the line is spoken to her sister.

passages.original: Sed propiora videamus. Cuiusnam modi est Superbi Tarquinii somnium, de quo in Bruto Accii loquitur ipse?
passages.english: But let us look at nearer things. Of what kind is the dream of Tarquin the Proud, about which he himself speaks in the Brutus of Accius?

passages.original: Est apud Platonem Socrates, cum esset in custodia publica, dicens Critoni, suo familiari, sibi post tertium diem esse moriendum; vidisse se in somnis pulchritudine eximia feminam, quae se nomine appellans diceret Homericum quendam eius modi versum: Tertia te Phthiae tempestas laeta locabit.
passages.english: In Plato there is Socrates, when he was in the public prison, saying to Crito, his friend, that he must die after the third day; [for] he had seen in his sleep a woman of outstanding beauty, who, calling him by name, spoke a Homeric line of this sort: "On the third day the fair season will set you in Phthia."

passages.original: ei visum in quiete egregia facie iuvenem dicere fore ut perbrevi convalesceret, paucisque diebus interiturum Alexandrum tyrannum, ipsum autem Eudemum quinquennio post domum esse rediturum. Atque ita quidem prima statim scribit Aristoteles consecuta, et convaluisse Eudemum, et ab uxoris fratribus interfectum tyrannum; quinto autem anno exeunte, cum esset spes ex illo somnio in Cyprum illum ex Sicilia esse rediturum, proeliantem eum ad Syracusas occidisse;
passages.english: [that] in his sleep a young man of outstanding appearance seemed to tell him that he would very soon recover, that the tyrant Alexander would perish within a few days, and that Eudemus himself would return home five years later. And indeed, Aristotle writes, the first things followed at once: Eudemus recovered, and the tyrant was killed by his wife's brothers; but at the end of the fifth year, when there was hope from that dream that he would return from Sicily to Cyprus, he fell fighting near Syracuse;

passages.original: Marium cum fascibus laureatis quaerere ex te, quid tristis esses, cumque tu te patria vi pulsum esse dixisses, prehendisse eum dextram tuam et bono animo te iussisse esse lictorique proxumo tradidisse, ut te in monumentum suum deduceret, et dixisse in eo tibi salutem fore. Tum et se exclamasse Sallustius narrat reditum tibi celerem et gloriosum paratum, et te ipsum visum somnio delectari. Nam illud mihi ipsi celeriter nuntiatum est, ut audivisses in monumento Marii de tuo reditu magnificentissumum illud senatus consultum esse factum referente optumo et clarissumo viro consule, idque frequentissimo theatro incredibili clamore et plausu comprobatum, dixisse te nihil illo Atinati somnio fieri posse divinius.
passages.english: [that] Gaius Marius, with his laurelled fasces, asked you why you were sad, and when you had said that you had been driven from your country by force, he took your right hand, told you to be of good heart, and handed you over to the nearest lictor to lead you to his monument, and said that there your safety would lie. Then, Sallustius relates, he himself exclaimed that a swift and glorious return had been prepared for you, and you yourself seemed delighted by the dream. For it was quickly reported to me myself that, when you had heard that the splendid decree of the senate concerning your return had been passed in the monument of Marius, on the motion of the consul, a most excellent and distinguished man, and that it had been approved in a packed theatre with incredible shouting and applause, you said that nothing could be more divine than that dream at Atina.
passages.notes: The 'monument of Marius' is a temple built by Marius (of Honos and Virtus). The 'C.' at the end of the context belongs with 'Marium'.

passages.original: Divinare autem morientes illo etiam exemplo confirmat Posidonius, quod adfert, Rhodium quendam morientem sex aequales nominasse et dixisse, qui primus eorum, qui secundus, qui deinde deinceps moriturus esset. Sed tribus modis censet deorum adpulsu homines somniare, uno, quod provideat animus ipse per sese, quippe qui deorum cognatione teneatur, altero, quod plenus aër sit inmortalium animorum, in quibus tamquam insignitae notae veritatis appareant, tertio, quod ipsi di cum dormientibus conloquantur.
passages.english: Posidonius also confirms that the dying divine by this example, which he cites: that a certain Rhodian, when dying, named six of his contemporaries and said which of them would die first, which second, and which next in order after that. But he holds that men dream by the impulse of the gods in three ways: one, because the soul foresees by itself, since it is bound by kinship with the gods; another, because the air is full of immortal souls, in which marks of truth appear as if stamped on them; the third, because the gods themselves converse with sleepers.

passages.original: Quorum alia sunt posita in monumentis et disciplina, quod Etruscorum declarant et haruspicini et fulgurales et rituales libri, vestri etiam augurales, alia autem subito ex tempore coniectura explicantur, ut apud Homerum Calchas, qui ex passerum numero belli Troiani annos auguratus est, et ut in Sullae scriptum historia videmus, quod te inspectante factum est, ut, cum ille in agro Nolano inmolaret ante praetorium, ab infima ara subito anguis emergeret, cum quidem C.
passages.english: Of these, some are set down in records and in a formal discipline, as the Etruscan books on haruspicy, on lightning, and on ritual show, and also your augural books; others are worked out suddenly, on the spot, by conjecture, like Calchas in Homer, who foretold the years of the Trojan War from the number of sparrows, and as we see written in the history of Sulla, about what happened while you were watching: when he was sacrificing in front of his headquarters in the territory of Nola, a snake suddenly came out from the bottom of the altar, and indeed Gaius
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off at 'C.', continuing with 'Postumius the haruspex' in the following passage.

passages.original: Fit etiam saepe specie quadam, saepe vocum gravitate et cantibus ut pellantur animi vehementius, saepe etiam cura et timore, qualis est illa Flexánima tamquam lýmphata aut Bacchí sacris Commóta in tumulis Teúcrum commemoráns suum. Atque etiam illa concitatio declarat vim in animis esse divinam. Negat enim sine furore Democritus quemquam poëtam magnum esse posse, quod idem dicit Plato. Quem, si placet, appellet furorem, dum modo is furor ita laudetur, ut in Phaedro Platonis laudatus est. Quid? vestra oratio in causis, quid? ipsa actio potest esse vehemens et gravis et copiosa, nisi est animus ipse commotior?
passages.english:
It also often happens that minds are stirred more violently by some sight, often by the depth of voices and by songs, often too by anxiety and fear, as is that [woman]:
Her mind distraught, as if possessed, or stirred
by Bacchus' rites among the tombs,
calling on her Teucer.
And this excitement too shows that there is a divine power in minds. For Democritus denies that anyone can be a great poet without madness, and Plato says the same. Let him call it madness if he likes, provided that this madness is praised as it was praised in Plato's Phaedrus. What of your speaking in lawsuits, what of your delivery itself: can it be vehement, weighty and abundant unless the mind itself is more than usually stirred?
passages.notes: The verse quotation is from an early Roman tragedy (unattributed here); the speaker is a woman lamenting Teucer.

passages.original: Quis est autem, quem non moveat clarissumis monumentis testata consignataque antiquitas? Calchantem augurem scribit Homerus longe optumum, eumque ducem classium fuisse ad Ilium, auspiciorum credo scientia, non locorum.
passages.english: And who is there who is not moved by antiquity attested and sealed by the most illustrious records? Homer writes that Calchas was by far the best augur, and that he was the leader of the fleets to Ilium, by his knowledge, I suppose, of auspices, not of places.

passages.original: Amphilochus et Mopsus Argivorum reges fuerunt, sed iidem augures, iique urbis in ora marituma Ciliciae Graecas condiderunt; atque etiam ante hos Amphiaraus et Tiresias non humiles et obscuri neque eorum similes, ut apud Ennium est, Quí sui quaestus caúsa fictas súscitant senténtias, sed clari et praestantes viri, qui avibus et signis admoniti futura dicebant; quorum de altero etiam apud inferos Homerus ait solum sapere, ceteros umbrarum vagari modo; Amphiaraum autem sic honoravit fama Graeciae, deus ut haberetur, atque ut ab eius solo, in quo est humatus, oracla peterentur.
passages.english: Amphilochus and Mopsus were kings of the Argives, but they were also augurs, and they founded Greek cities on the sea coast of Cilicia; and even before these, Amphiaraus and Tiresias were not lowly and obscure men, nor like those who, as Ennius has it, "for the sake of their own gain stir up fabricated pronouncements," but famous and outstanding men, who, warned by birds and signs, foretold the future; of one of whom Homer says that even among the dead he alone is wise, while the rest merely wander as shades; and Amphiaraus the renown of Greece so honoured that he was held to be a god, and that oracles were sought from the ground in which he was buried.

passages.original: Atque ille Romuli auguratus pastoralis, non urbanus fuit nec fictus ad opiniones inperitorum, sed a certis acceptus et posteris traditus. Itaque Romulus augur, ut apud Ennium est, cum fratre item augure Curantes magna cum cura tum cupientes Regni dant operam simul auspicio augurioque.†In monte Remus auspicio se devovet atque secundam Solus avem servat. At Romulus pulcher in alto Quaerit Aventino, servat genus altivolantum.Certabant, urbem Romam Remoramne vocarent.Omnibus cura viris, uter esset induperator.Exspectant;
passages.english: And that augury of Romulus was a shepherd's, not a city one, nor invented to suit the opinions of the ignorant, but received from reliable [sources] and handed down to posterity. So Romulus the augur, as Ennius has it, with his brother, likewise an augur: "Taking great care then, both desiring kingship, / they apply themselves together to auspice and augury. / On a hill Remus devotes himself to the auspice and alone / watches for a favourable bird. But handsome Romulus on the lofty / Aventine seeks, watches for the race of high-flyers. / They were contending whether to call the city Roma or Remora. / All the men were anxious which of the two would be ruler. / They wait;
passages.notes: The edition marks a crux (†) before "In monte"; the text of that line is doubtful. Some editors place Remus on the Aventine and Romulus elsewhere.

passages.original: Idemque mittit et signa nobis eius generis, qualia permulta historia tradidit, quale scriptum illud videmus: si luna paulo ante solis ortum defecisset in signo Leonis, fore ut armis Dareus et Persae ab Alexandro et Macedonibus proelio vincerentur Dareusque moreretur, et, si puella nata biceps esset, seditionem in populo fore, corruptelam et adulterium domi, et, si mulier leonem peperisse visa esset, fore ut ab exteris gentibus vinceretur ea res publica, in qua id contigisset. Eiusdem generis etiam illud est, quod scribit Herodotus, Croesi filium, cum esset infans, locutum; quo ostento regnum patris et domum funditus concidisse. Caput arsisse Servio Tullio dormienti quae historia non prodidit? Ut igitur, qui se tradidit quieti praeparato animo cum bonis cogitationibus, tum rebus ad tranquillitatem adcommodatis, certa et vera cernit in somnis, sic castus animus purusque vigilantis et ad astrorum et ad avium reliquorumque signorum et ad extorum veritatem est paratior.
passages.english: And the same [power] also sends us signs of the kind that history has handed down in great numbers, such as the one we see written: that if the moon were eclipsed shortly before sunrise in the sign of Leo, Darius and the Persians would be defeated in battle by Alexander and the Macedonians, and Darius would die; and that if a girl were born with two heads, there would be sedition among the people, and seduction and adultery in the home; and that if a woman seemed to have given birth to a lion, the state in which this happened would be conquered by foreign nations. Of the same kind is what Herodotus writes, that the son of Croesus spoke when he was an infant, and that by this portent his father's kingdom and house utterly fell. What history has not recorded that Servius Tullius' head blazed while he slept? Therefore, just as one who has given himself to rest with a mind prepared both by good thoughts and by things suited to tranquillity sees sure and true things in his sleep, so a chaste and pure mind, when awake, is better prepared for the truth of the stars, of birds, of other signs, and of entrails.

passages.original: Scriptum est item, cum Critonis, sui familiaris, oculum alligatum vidisset, quaesivisse, quid esset; cum autem ille respondisset in agro ambulanti ramulum adductum, ut remissus esset, in oculum suum recidisse, tum Socrates: Non enim paruisti mihi revocanti, cum uterer, qua soleo, praesagitione divina. Idem etiam Socrates, cum apud Delium male pugnatum esset Lachete praetore fugeretque cum ipso Lachete, ut ventum est in trivium, eadem, qua ceteri, fugere noluit.
passages.english: It is likewise written that, when he had seen the eye of Crito, his friend, bandaged, he asked what it was; and when Crito answered that while he was walking in the country a branch that had been pulled back, when it was let go, sprang back into his eye, then Socrates [said]: "That is because you did not obey me when I called you back, using the divine presentiment I usually use." The same Socrates too, when the battle at Delium had gone badly under the command of Laches and he was fleeing with Laches himself, when they came to a place where three roads met, refused to flee by the same road as the others.

passages.original: Quocirca primum mihi videtur, ut Posidonius facit, a deo, de quo satis dictum est, deinde a fato, deinde a natura vis omnis divinandi ratioque repetenda. Fieri igitur omnia fato ratio cogit fateri. Fatum autem id appello, quod Graeci εἱμαρμένην, id est ordinem seriemque causarum, cum causae causa nexa rem ex se gignat.
passages.english: Therefore it seems to me that, as Posidonius does, the whole force and principle of divination should be traced first from god, of whom enough has been said, then from fate, then from nature. Reason, then, compels us to admit that all things happen by fate. And I call fate what the Greeks call heimarmenē, that is, an order and series of causes, when cause linked to cause produces a thing from itself.

passages.original: Democritus autem censet sapienter instituisse veteres, ut hostiarum immolatarum inspicerentur exta; quorum ex habitu atque ex colore tum salubritatis, tum pestilentiae signa percipi, non numquam etiam, quae sit vel sterilitas agrorum vel fertilitas futura.
passages.english: Democritus, moreover, holds that the ancients acted wisely in establishing that the entrails of sacrificed victims should be inspected; from their condition and colour, [he says,] signs are perceived now of healthiness, now of pestilence, and sometimes even of what barrenness or fertility of the fields is to come.

passages.original: addunt ad extremum omnia levius casura rebus divinis procuratis; si enim nihil fit extra fatum, nihil levari re divina potest. Hoc sentit Homerus, cum querentem Iovem inducit, quod Sarpedonem filium a morte contra fatum eripere non posset. Hoc idem significat Graecus ille in eam sententiam versus: Quod fóre paratum est, íd summum exsuperát Iovem.
passages.english:
Finally they add that all things will fall out more lightly once rites have been performed to avert them; but if nothing happens outside fate, nothing can be lightened by a rite. Homer means this when he brings in Jupiter complaining that he could not snatch his son Sarpedon from death against fate. The same is signified by that Greek verse to this effect:
What is set to be, that overpowers even highest Jupiter.

passages.original: sed tamen eo concesso qui evenit, ut is, qui impetrire velit, convenientem hostiam rebus suis immolet? Hoc erat, quod ego non rebar posse dissolvi. At quam festive dissolvitur! pudet me non tui quidem, cuius etiam memoriam admiror, sed Chrysippi, Antipatri, Posidonii, qui idem istuc quidem dicunt, quod est dictum a te, ad hostiam deligendam ducem esse vim quandam sentientem atque divinam, quae toto confusa mundo sit. Illud vero multo etiam melius, quod et a te usurpatum est et dicitur ab illis: cum immolare quispiam velit, tum fieri extorum mutationem, ut aut absit aliquid aut supersit;
passages.english: But even granting that, how does it come about that the one who wishes to obtain a favourable omen sacrifices a victim suited to his affairs? This was what I thought could not be resolved. But how wittily it is resolved! I am ashamed, not of you indeed, whose memory I even admire, but of Chrysippus, Antipater, Posidonius, who say exactly what was said by you, that in choosing the victim the guide is a certain sentient and divine force which is diffused through the whole world. But that is much better still, which was both adopted by you and is said by them: that when someone wishes to sacrifice, then a change of the entrails takes place, so that something is either missing or superfluous;
passages.notes: "impetrire" is the augural term for obtaining favourable signs.

passages.original: Democritus quidem optumis verbis causam explicat, cur ante lucem galli canant; depulso enim de pectore et in omne corpus diviso et mitificato cibo cantus edere quiete satiatos; qui quidem silentio noctis, ut ait Ennius, favent faucíbus russis Cantú plausuque premúnt alas. Cum igitur hoc animal tam sit canorum sua sponte, quid in mentem venit Callistheni dicere deos gallis signum dedisse cantandi, cum id vel natura vel casus efficere potuisset?
passages.english: Democritus, indeed, explains in excellent words the reason why cocks crow before dawn: for when the food has been pushed down from the chest and distributed through the whole body and softened, they utter their songs, sated with rest; and they, in the silence of the night, as Ennius says, "give play to their ruddy throats in song, and beat their wings with a clapping." Since, then, this creature is so given to song of its own accord, what came into Callisthenes' mind to say that the gods had given the cocks a signal to crow, when either nature or chance could have brought that about?
passages.notes: The Ennius verses are corrupt in the transmitted text ("favent faucibus russis / cantu plausuque premunt alas"); the rendering of "favent" and "premunt alas" is uncertain.

passages.original: Nam illud mirarer, si crederem, quod apud Homerum Calchantem dixisti ex passerum numero belli Troiani annos auguratum; de cuius coniectura sic apud Homerum, ut nos otiosi convertimus, loquitur Agamemnon: Ferte, viri, et duros animo tolerate labores,Auguris ut nostri Calchantis fata queamus Scire ratosne habeant an vanos pectoris orsus.Namque omnes memori portentum mente retentant,Qui non funestis liquerunt lumina fatis.Argolicis primum ut vestita est classibus Aulis,Quae Priamo cladem et Troiae pestemque ferebant,Nos circum latices gelidos fumantibus aris Aurigeris divom placantes numina tauris Sub platano umbrifera, fons unde emanat aquai+,Vidimus inmani specie tortuque draconem Terribilem, Iovis ut pulsu penetraret ab ara;Qui platani in ramo foliorum tegmine saeptos Corripuit pullos;
passages.english: For I would marvel at that, if I believed it, which you said: that in Homer Calchas foretold the years of the Trojan War from the number of sparrows. Of his interpretation Agamemnon speaks thus in Homer, as I rendered it in my leisure: "Bear up, men, and endure hard labours in your spirit, so that we may know whether the prophecies of our augur Calchas hold firm, or whether the promptings of his breast are empty. For all retain the portent in mindful memory who have not left the light through deadly fates. When Aulis first was clothed with the Argive fleets, which were bearing slaughter to Priam and ruin to Troy, we, around the cool springs, on smoking altars, appeasing the divine power of the gods with gold-horned bulls beneath a shady plane tree, from where a spring of water flows, saw a serpent, terrible in its monstrous form and coiling, which, at the impulse of Jupiter, made its way from the altar; it seized the nestlings shut in by the covering of leaves on a branch of the plane tree;
passages.notes: The '+' after 'aquai' is the edition's mark of a corrupt or doubtful reading; translated as 'water'. 'Calchantis fata' rendered as 'prophecies'.

passages.original: Quae autem est inter augures conveniens et coniuncta constantia? Ad nostri augurii consuetudinem dixit Ennius: Tum tonuit laevum bene tempestate serena. At Homericus Aiax apud Achillem querens de ferocitate Troianorum nescio quid hoc modo nuntiat: Prospera Iuppiter his dextris fulgoribus edit. Ita nobis sinistra videntur, Graiis et barbaris dextra meliora.
passages.english: And what consistent and harmonious agreement is there among augurs? In keeping with the custom of our augury Ennius said: "Then it thundered on the left, auspiciously, in clear weather." But Homer's Ajax, complaining to Achilles about the ferocity of the Trojans, reports something in this way: "Jupiter gives them favourable signs with lightning on the right." So to us things on the left seem better, to Greeks and barbarians things on the right.

passages.original: illudne dubium est, quin multi, cum ita nati essent, ut quaedam contra naturam depravata haberent, restituerentur et corrigerentur ab natura, cum se ipsa revocasset, aut arte atque medicina? ut, quorum linguae sic inhaererent, ut loqui non possent, eae scalpello resectae liberarentur. Multi etiam naturae vitium meditatione atque exercitatione sustulerunt, ut Demosthenem scribit Phalereus, cum rho dicere nequiret, exercitatione fecisse, ut planissume diceret. Quodsi haec astro ingenerata et tradita essent, nulla res ea mutare posset. Quid? dissimilitudo locorum nonne dissimilis hominum procreationes habet?
passages.english: Is it doubtful that many, when they had been born such that they had certain things deformed contrary to nature, were restored and corrected by nature, when she had recovered herself, or by art and medicine? For instance, those whose tongues were so tied down that they could not speak were freed by having them cut loose with a scalpel. Many too have removed a natural defect by practice and exercise, as Phalereus writes that Demosthenes, when he could not pronounce rho, brought it about by exercise that he pronounced it most clearly. But if these things had been implanted and handed down by a star, nothing could change them. What then? Does not the difference of places produce different breeds of men?

passages.original: Quis enim est, qui credat Apollinis ex oraculo Pyrrho esse responsum: Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse? Primum Latine Apollo numquam locutus est; deinde ista sors inaudita Graecis est; praeterea Pyrrhi temporibus iam Apollo versus facere desierat; postremo, quamquam semper fuit, ut apud Ennium est, stolidum genus Aeacidarum,Bellipotentes sunt magis quam sapientipotentes, tamen hanc amphiboliam versus intellegere potuisset, vincere te Romanos nihilo magis in se quam in Romanos valere; nam illa amphibolia, quae Croesum decepit, vel Chrysippum potuisset fallere, haec vero ne Epicurum quidem.
passages.english: For who is there who would believe that this reply was given to Pyrrhus from the oracle of Apollo: "I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, the Romans can conquer"? First, Apollo never spoke Latin; next, that oracle is unheard of among the Greeks; besides, by Pyrrhus' time Apollo had already stopped making verses; finally, although the race of the Aeacidae was always, as it is in Ennius, dull-witted — "They are mighty in war rather than mighty in wisdom" — still he could have understood the ambiguity of this verse, that "you the Romans conquer" applied no more to himself than to the Romans; for that ambiguity which deceived Croesus could have fooled even Chrysippus, but this one not even Epicurus.
passages.notes: The Latin oracle "Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse" is grammatically ambiguous (either Pyrrhus conquers the Romans or the Romans conquer him); the English attempts to keep the ambiguity.

passages.original: Utrum igitur censemus dormientium animos per sene ipsos in somniando moveri an, ut Democritus censet, externa et adventicia visione pulsari? Sive enim sic est sive illo modo, videri possunt permulta somniantibus falsa pro veris. Nam et navigantibus moveri videntur ea, quae stant, et quodam obtutu oculorum duo pro uno lucernae lumina.
passages.english: Do we, then, think that the minds of sleepers are moved of themselves in dreaming, or, as Democritus thinks, are struck by an external and adventitious vision? For whichever way it is, very many false things can appear to dreamers as true. For to people sailing, things that stand still seem to move, and by a certain way of looking with the eyes two flames of a lamp [seem to appear] instead of one.
passages.notes: 'per sene ipsos' read as 'per se ipsi/ipsos' (scanning error).

passages.original: Iam vero quis dicere audeat vera omnia esse somnia? Aliquot somnia vera, inquit Ennius, sed omnia noenum necesse est. Quae est tandem ista distinctio? quae vera, quae falsa habet? et, si vera a deo mittuntur, falsa unde nascuntur? nam si ea quoque divina, quid inconstantius deo? quid inscitius autem est quam mentes mortalium falsis et mendacibus visis concitare?
passages.english: Now who would dare to say that all dreams are true? "Some dreams are true," says Ennius, "but not necessarily all." What, pray, is that distinction? Which does he hold true, which false? And if the true ones are sent by a god, where do the false ones arise from? For if those too are divine, what is more inconsistent than a god? And what is more ignorant than to stir up the minds of mortals with false and lying visions?

passages.original: Naturam autem eam dico, qua numquam animus insistens agitatione et motu esse vacuus potest. Is cum languore corporis nec membris uti nec sensibus potest, incidit in visa varia et incerta ex reliquiis, ut ait Aristoteles, inhaerentibus earum rerum, quas vigilans gesserit aut cogitaverit; quarum perturbatione mirabiles interdum existunt species somniorum; quae si alia falsa, alia vera, qua nota internoscantur, scire sane velim.
passages.english: I mean by nature that by which the mind, never at rest, can never be free of agitation and motion. When, through the languor of the body, it can use neither limbs nor senses, it falls into varied and uncertain visions arising, as Aristotle says, from the lingering remnants of the things it did or thought while awake; and from the disturbance of these, wondrous forms of dreams sometimes arise. If some of these are false and others true, I should very much like to know by what mark they are distinguished.

passages.original: Chrysippus quidem divinationem definit his verbis: vim cognoscentem et videntem et explicantem signa, quae a dis hominibus portendantur; officium autem esse eius praenoscere, dei erga homines mente qua sint quidque significent, quem ad modumque ea procurentur atque expientur. Idemque somniorum coniectionem definit hoc modo: esse vim cernentem et explanantem, quae a dis hominibus significentur in somnis. Quid ergo? ad haec mediocri opus est prudentia an et ingenio praestanti et eruditione perfecta?
passages.english: Chrysippus, indeed, defines divination in these words: a power that recognises, sees and explains the signs that are portended to men by the gods; and its function, he says, is to know in advance with what disposition the gods are toward men, what [the signs] signify, and in what way they are to be averted and expiated. And he likewise defines the interpretation of dreams in this way: that it is a power that discerns and explains what is signified to men by the gods in dreams. What then? Is moderate good sense needed for these things, or both outstanding talent and perfect learning?

passages.original: quam multi inopes digni praesidio deorum nullo somnio ad thensaurum reperiendum admonentur! Quam autem ob causam tam est obscure admonitus, ut ex ovo nasceretur thensauri similitudo, potius quam aperte thensaurum quaerere iuberetur, sicut aperte Simonides vetitus est navigare?
passages.english: How many poor people worthy of the gods' protection are prompted by no dream to find a treasure! And for what reason was he prompted so obscurely, so that a likeness of treasure arose from an egg, rather than being openly told to look for treasure, just as Simonides was openly forbidden to sail?

passages.original: Quem enim tu Marium visum a me putas? Speciem, credo, eius et imaginem, ut Democrito videtur. Unde profectam imaginem? a corporibus enim solidis et a certis figuris vult fluere imagines; quod igitur Marii corpus erat? Ex eo, inquit, quod fuerat. Ista igitur me imago Marii in campum Atinatem persequebatur?—Plena sunt imaginum omnia;
passages.english: For what Marius do you think I saw? His form, I suppose, and image, as Democritus holds. From where did the image come? For he holds that images flow from solid bodies and definite shapes; what body of Marius, then, was there? From the one, he says, that had been. So that image of Marius was following me into the plain of Atina? — "All things are full of images;
